title: One Semantic Layer, Shared by BI and AI
purpose: Show how OneLake data stores feed a shared, certified semantic model that both Power BI reporting and AI consumers (Fabric data agents, Copilot) read from the same governed definition, instead of each consumer re-deriving its own metrics.
accessibleSummary: An architecture diagram in three lanes. OneLake data stores (lakehouse and warehouse Delta tables) feed a semantic model built in Direct Lake mode. The model layer adds endorsed measures, row-level security, and framing control. A Fabric IQ ontology sits alongside the model, mapping business concepts onto it without moving data. From there, four consumption surfaces read the same governed layer: Power BI reports, Analyze in Excel, Copilot, and a Fabric data agent. A warning node calls out the Direct Lake framing lag as a freshness limit every consumer inherits.
longDescription: This is a converge-then-fan-out architecture. Two OneLake-backed stores — lakehouse Delta tables and warehouse Delta tables — both feed one semantic model, because both physically write the same open Delta format. The semantic model is built in Direct Lake mode, reading those Delta tables directly with no import step. On top of the model, endorsed measures and row-level security are defined once. A Fabric IQ ontology (preview) can be generated or aligned directly from that same semantic model, adding a business-concept layer without duplicating data. From there the diagram fans out to four consumption surfaces that all read the identical governed model: Power BI reports and dashboards, Analyze in Excel, Copilot experiences, and a Fabric data agent that translates natural-language questions into DAX against the model. A warning node captures the one freshness limit every consumer inherits from Direct Lake: results reflect the last framing operation, not the live table.

nodes.label: Lakehouse Delta tables
nodes.summary: Spark-managed gold tables in OneLake, stored as Delta.
nodes.detail: A Fabric lakehouse merges lake-scale storage with warehouse-style querying: structured data lives in managed Delta tables that both Spark and T-SQL can read with no data movement. These gold tables are the typical source for a governed semantic model.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because the lakehouse writes Delta directly to OneLake, the semantic model downstream can read it in Direct Lake mode with no separate export or copy step.

evidence.note: A Fabric lakehouse merges data-lake scale storage with warehouse-style querying: structured and unstructured data live in one location and can be analyzed with both Apache Spark and T-SQL, with no data movement between systems.

inputs: Bronze/silver Spark transformations landing gold tables in the Tables area
processing: Fabric auto-registers Delta writes in the metastore
Tables become immediately queryable via Spark SQL or the SQL analytics endpoint
outputs: Queryable gold Delta tables ready to be modelled into a semantic model
drill.example: A Spark job publishes gold_sales as a Delta table; the semantic model author picks it up directly from OneLake with no export step.
controls: Which tables are promoted to gold and exposed for modelling
Table naming/schema conventions the model will bind to
failureModes: Modelling directly on ungoverned bronze/silver tables instead of a stable gold contract, so upstream schema churn breaks the model

nodes.label: Warehouse Delta tables
nodes.summary: T-SQL-managed star schema tables, also stored as Delta in OneLake.
nodes.detail: Fabric Data Warehouse tables are physically Delta tables — Parquet files plus a transaction log — and are automatically published to OneLake in Delta format, so they are readable by other engines without export jobs, exactly like lakehouse tables.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because both stores write the same Delta format, a semantic model can be built from either — or both, via a composite model — without caring which engine populated the data.

evidence.note: Warehouse tables are physically stored as Delta tables (Parquet data files plus a file-based transaction log), the same open format used for all Fabric data, and warehouse data is automatically published to OneLake Files in Delta format.

inputs: T-SQL-loaded star schema tables (COPY INTO, pipelines, cross-database CTAS)
processing: Multi-table ACID transactions commit fact and dimension loads
Tables persist as Delta and publish to OneLake automatically
outputs: A governed relational star schema, open as Delta, ready for the semantic model
drill.example: A nightly load commits a fact table and three dimensions inside one warehouse transaction; the resulting Delta tables are immediately visible to the semantic model layer.
controls: Star schema grain and dimension conformance
Which warehouse tables are exposed to modelling vs kept as staging
failureModes: Building the semantic model on staging/ETL tables instead of the curated star schema, exposing transient data

nodes.label: Semantic model (Direct Lake)
nodes.summary: One tabular model reading Delta tables directly from OneLake, no import required.
nodes.detail: The semantic model is a data model built on Analysis Services tabular technology. In Direct Lake mode it reads Delta Parquet data straight from OneLake, giving import-mode query speed without maintaining a separately refreshed copy.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single governed definition point: one model, one set of relationships and measures, read by every downstream consumer instead of each report or agent re-deriving its own logic.

evidence.note: A semantic model is a data source prepared for reporting and visualization; apart from streaming models, every semantic model is a data model built on Analysis Services tabular modeling technology.

Direct Lake is a semantic-model storage mode in which the model reads Delta tables straight from OneLake, avoiding both data import and DirectQuery, pairing import-like performance with DirectQuery-like freshness.

inputs: Lakehouse and/or warehouse Delta tables selected for modelling
processing: Define relationships between fact and dimension tables
Set the model to Direct Lake storage mode
Build DAX measures once at the model layer
outputs: A live, queryable tabular model with no refresh schedule to operate
drill.example: A revenue model relates a Direct Lake fact table to conformed customer, product, and date dimensions, with a single Total Revenue measure every report reuses.
controls: Direct Lake flavor (on OneLake vs on SQL)
Which tables use Direct Lake vs Import in a composite model
failureModes: Redefining the same measure per report instead of centralizing it in the model, producing inconsistent numbers across teams

nodes.label: Endorsed measures & RLS
nodes.summary: Certified/promoted status, shared measures, and row-level security applied once at the model.
nodes.detail: Endorsement signals trustworthiness: item owners can self-apply Promoted status, and organizations can apply Certified status to items meeting quality standards, with endorsed items receiving priority placement in search and catalog views. Row-level security roles are either dynamic, filtering by the report user's identity, or static, applying one fixed filter.
nodes.whyItMatters: Certifying the model and applying RLS here — once — means every consumption surface downstream inherits the same trust signal and the same security boundary, rather than each surface implementing its own.

evidence.note: Endorsement provides two levels of item trustworthiness signaling: item owners can self-apply Promoted status, while organizations can apply Certified status to items that meet defined quality standards; endorsed items receive priority placement in certain search results and catalog views.
Row-level security roles in a semantic model are either dynamic, filtering data based on the identity of the report user, or static, applying one fixed filter to every user assigned to the role.

inputs: The built semantic model, before it is discoverable across the tenant
processing: Apply Certified or Promoted endorsement
Define dynamic or static RLS roles
Publish endorsed measures with clear names and descriptions
outputs: A trusted, secured model surfaced in the OneLake catalog for reuse
drill.example: Finance certifies the revenue model and defines a dynamic RLS role scoping regional managers to their own region; every report, Excel workbook, and agent query built on the model inherits that scoping automatically.
failureModes: Certifying a model before RLS is tested, exposing rows the endorsement badge implies are safe to trust broadly

nodes.label: Fabric IQ ontology (preview)
nodes.summary: Business concepts and relationships mapped onto the semantic model, without moving data.
nodes.detail: Ontologies in Fabric IQ can be generated or aligned directly from Power BI semantic models already in production, so business terms and KPIs stay consistent across reports, agents, and applications instead of being redefined per experience. The ontology adds a business-entity layer on top of the model — it does not duplicate the underlying data.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without a shared ontology, every business question otherwise requires manual translation by a domain expert from raw tables and schemas into business concepts — the ontology is what lets an AI agent ask 'revenue' and get the same answer the certified model already defines.

evidence.note: Ontologies in Fabric IQ can be generated or aligned directly from Power BI semantic models already in production, so business terms and KPIs stay consistent across reports, agents, and applications instead of being redefined per experience.

inputs: The certified semantic model's tables, relationships, and measures
processing: Generate or align ontology entities, relationships, and rules from the model
Expose a natural-language query layer (NL2Ontology)
outputs: A business-concept layer that agents and Copilot can reason over
drill.example: The ontology declares 'Customer' and 'Order' as entities with a relationship, reusing the same joins already defined in the semantic model rather than re-deriving them.
controls: Which model entities are exposed in the ontology
Keeping the ontology in sync as the model evolves
failureModes: Letting the ontology drift out of sync with model changes, so agent answers reference stale relationships

nodes.label: Direct Lake freshness is framing-bound
nodes.summary: Every consumer reads data as of the last framing operation, not the live table.
nodes.detail: Direct Lake queries reflect the Delta table state as of the most recent successful framing operation, not the live table, so writes landing after the last frame remain invisible until the next one. This limit applies uniformly to every consumer of the shared model — reports, Excel, Copilot, and the data agent all see the same framing point.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because the whole point of this architecture is one shared definition, a framing lag is not a per-report quirk — it is a property every consumer inherits at once, so it needs to be understood centrally rather than debugged per surface.

evidence.note: Direct Lake queries reflect the Delta table state as of the most recent successful framing operation, not the live table, so writes landing after the last frame remain invisible until the next one.

inputs: A Direct Lake semantic model with automatic-updates reframing enabled or disabled
processing: Underlying Delta table receives new writes
Model does not see them until the next framing event re-binds to the current Parquet file set
outputs: A shared, potentially stale view across every consumption surface until the next frame
drill.example: A late-arriving sales correction lands in the warehouse at 9:05am; the model's last frame was 9:00am, so the data agent, Power BI report, and Excel workbook all report the pre-correction number until the next frame runs.
controls: Automatic-updates toggle (on by default) vs deliberate manual/scheduled framing
Pinning framing points during mid-ETL windows for consistency
failureModes: Assuming Direct Lake means live data because there's no refresh schedule to point at
Disabling automatic updates for ETL consistency and forgetting to re-enable it, freezing every consumer's view

nodes.label: Power BI reports & dashboards
nodes.summary: Interactive reports live-connected to the certified model.
nodes.detail: Reports built on a published semantic model use a live connection, so the report can be authored and edited without changing the model itself; at least Build permission on the model is required to live-connect.
nodes.whyItMatters: Live connection means report authors reuse the certified model's measures and RLS exactly as defined, rather than importing a private copy that can drift.

evidence.note: Reports built on a published semantic model use a live connection, so the report can be authored and edited without changing the model itself; at least Build permission on the model is required to live-connect.

processing: Author visuals against the live-connected model
Optionally add report-level measures without touching the shared model
outputs: Interactive reports and dashboards distributed via Power BI apps
drill.example: A regional sales dashboard live-connects to the certified revenue model; a report-level measure adds a custom KPI without modifying the shared model for other consumers.
controls: Build permission gating who can live-connect
Report-level measures kept local vs promoted back into the model
failureModes: A report author lacking Build permission falling back to importing a private copy, fragmenting the single definition

nodes.label: Analyze in Excel
nodes.summary: Refreshable Excel pivot tables connected to the same model.
nodes.detail: Beyond interactive reports, a semantic model also serves paginated reports, data explorations, ad-hoc DAX queries, and refreshable Excel pivot or flat tables through the Analyze in Excel integration.
nodes.whyItMatters: Business analysts who prefer Excel still query the identical certified model rather than exporting a static extract, keeping their numbers consistent with every other consumer.

evidence.note: Beyond interactive reports, a semantic model also serves paginated reports, data explorations, ad-hoc DAX queries (including DAX query view), and refreshable Excel pivot or flat tables through the Analyze in Excel integration.

inputs: The certified semantic model, reachable via Analyze in Excel
processing: Excel connects a PivotTable directly to the model over the same live connection mechanism
outputs: Refreshable pivot tables reflecting the model's current framing point
drill.example: A finance analyst builds a PivotTable against the certified revenue model instead of requesting a CSV export from the data team.
controls: Read/Build permission on the model gating Excel access
failureModes: Analysts falling back to manual CSV exports when they lack model permission, recreating the ungoverned-copy problem this architecture exists to prevent

nodes.label: Copilot
nodes.summary: Fabric/Power BI Copilot generating summaries and visuals grounded in the certified model.
nodes.detail: Within Fabric, Power BI shares platform-level features with other workloads including Copilot, which generates natural-language summaries and assists in report building grounded in the underlying semantic model.
nodes.whyItMatters: Copilot answers are only as trustworthy as the model backing them; grounding it in the certified, RLS-secured model means its summaries respect the same security boundary as a human report author would.

evidence.note: Within Fabric, Power BI shares platform-level features with other workloads — OneLake integration, Direct Lake mode, Dataflows Gen2 and notebooks, Purview-based security and governance, Data Activator alerting, and Copilot.

inputs: Natural-language prompts against a report or model grounded in the certified semantic model
processing: Copilot generates DAX/visuals scoped to the requesting user's model permissions
outputs: AI-generated summaries and report scaffolding consistent with the certified model
drill.example: A user asks Copilot to summarize quarterly performance; the response draws on the same certified measures the finance-authored dashboard uses.
controls: Model certification as the trust signal Copilot answers inherit
failureModes: Users trusting a Copilot summary without realizing it is scoped by their own RLS view, missing context other roles see

nodes.label: Fabric data agent
nodes.summary: Conversational analytics translating natural language into DAX against the model.
nodes.detail: A Fabric data agent connects to governed OneLake data through lakehouses, warehouses, semantic models, and KQL databases, and after identifying the relevant source routes the question to a source-specific generator — NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models.
nodes.whyItMatters: Routing agent questions through NL2DAX against the certified model, rather than raw SQL against tables, means the agent's answers respect the exact same measures and RLS as every human-facing report.

evidence.note: After identifying the relevant data source, the agent routes the question to a source-specific generator: NL2SQL for lakehouse/warehouse, NL2DAX for Power BI semantic models, NL2KQL for KQL databases, or a Microsoft Graph query for organizational data.
The agent enforces read-only, least-privilege access by executing under the requesting user's own credentials and permissions, so each query only reaches data that user is already authorized to view.

inputs: A natural-language question and the certified semantic model as an attached data source
processing: Route the question to NL2DAX against the model
Execute the generated DAX under the requesting user's own credentials
drill.example: "What was Q3 revenue in the West region?" resolves through NL2DAX against the certified model's Total Revenue measure, scoped by the caller's RLS role.
controls: Which data sources (up to five) are attached to the agent
Instruction/example-query configuration to bias source selection
failureModes: Attaching an uncertified, ungoverned model to the agent, letting it answer from a definition that disagrees with the certified one

edges.label: certify, add measures, secure with RLS

walkthrough.title: Two stores, one open format
walkthrough.explanation: Lakehouse and warehouse tables both write Delta into OneLake, so either can feed the same downstream model.

walkthrough.title: The warehouse path is equally native
walkthrough.explanation: Warehouse tables are just as directly Delta-in-OneLake as lakehouse tables — the choice of store doesn't fragment the semantic layer.

walkthrough.title: One model, built in Direct Lake
walkthrough.explanation: The semantic model reads Delta tables directly with no import step, becoming the single point where relationships and measures are defined.

walkthrough.title: Certify and secure once
walkthrough.explanation: Endorsement and row-level security are applied at the model, so every downstream consumer inherits the same trust and access boundary automatically.

walkthrough.title: Ontology reuses the model, doesn't duplicate it
walkthrough.explanation: Fabric IQ can generate or align an ontology directly from the certified model, adding business-concept mapping without moving data.

walkthrough.title: Warning: the shared freshness limit
walkthrough.explanation: Every consumer of this architecture reads data as of the last framing operation — a limit worth understanding centrally, since it affects all four consumption surfaces at once.

walkthrough.title: Power BI live-connects
walkthrough.explanation: Reports read the certified model directly via live connection, inheriting its measures and RLS.

walkthrough.title: Excel reads the same model
walkthrough.explanation: Analyze in Excel gives business analysts a governed path instead of static exports.

walkthrough.title: Copilot is grounded, not generative-from-nothing
walkthrough.explanation: Copilot's summaries and visual suggestions are grounded in the same certified model, respecting the requesting user's RLS scope.

walkthrough.title: The agent closes the loop with NL2DAX
walkthrough.explanation: A Fabric data agent routes natural-language questions through NL2DAX against the model, using the Fabric IQ ontology's business concepts and executing under the caller's own credentials.
